a1_foot: The first counted station above Sarnhold is a lamp bracket, a bench, and a signing book on a chain, and the book has been signed every day this winter. Six ways go up the spine from here and all six of them reach the crown gate. The scouts' opinion, given in the map room, was that none of them is safe and two of them are worse than the others.
e_a1_foot_1: The book is signed and the road is refused in the same movement, which is at least honest arithmetic. The company walks back into Sarnhold before noon to explain a charter it will not be keeping. Thane accepts the report without argument and files it, and files the charter with it, and that is the end of the Ninth Sword as a company of record.
a1_switch: Nine switchbacks of dwarf paving climb out of the treeline in thaw meltwater running an inch deep over the stone. The drop grows behind each turn until the fortress is a grey mark below. A Guild train's ruts are a day old in the slush, and they cut every corner the company is looking at.
a1_switch_a: Corner-cutting on wet scree saves the best part of an hour and puts everybody's ankles on notice for the rest of the climb. Hask remarks that he has done exactly this on both his previous trips and paid for it both times. He does it again anyway, which tells the company something about Hask.
a1_switch_b: The paving is taken properly, turn by wide turn, in meltwater that has opinions about boot leather and none at all about the company's schedule. It costs an hour. Nobody turns an ankle, nobody goes down, and the barrow arrives at the scree field upright with its load still lashed.
a1_switch_c: The company is roped through four exposed turns on Vurma's insistence, which costs a half hour and makes everybody feel faintly ridiculous. On the third turn Mira's feet go out from under her on glazed stone. She goes down eleven inches instead of two hundred feet, and after that nobody mentions the rope again.
e_a1_switch_1: The switchbacks are run in the last of the light, with meltwater going to glass behind every boot as the temperature drops. The fourth turn has been refusing that pace since the legion cut it. It refuses it again, and the company hears the fall for a long time afterwards without being able to see any of it.
e_a1_switch_2: The last corner is cut over the drop because the first four worked, which is how the road takes people. The scree there is scree over ice over nothing at all. The company hears it happen rather than sees it, and the sound stops before anybody has finished turning round.
a1_scree: A live scree field crosses the road for two hundred yards, moving quietly on its own account in the thaw. The Guild train's wheel-track runs into the middle of it and does not come out the other side, which is the single most informative thing anybody has seen since the treeline.
a1_scree_a: Five separate crossings at a walking pace, one person at a time, with the field talking under everybody's boots the whole way. It takes ninety minutes. It gets five people and one barrow across a moving slope that swallowed a Guild wagon, which is the entire argument for doing it slowly.
a1_scree_b: The field is crossed at a run, all five together while it is quiet, and it stays quiet for the whole two hundred yards. It costs the company its wind and one reservoir lamp, which goes down the slope in eleven bounces and is still audible after it is out of sight.
e_a1_scree_1: The drainage culvert under the scree field is four feet high, half full of meltwater, and entirely full of the reason the Guild train's wheel-track stops in the middle of the field above it. The company is nine feet inside before anybody's lamp reaches the far end of what is in there with them.
a1_cairn: A cairn stands at the third station's turning, built not of loose stone but of station-book pages weighted under one flat slab. The top page has nine names on it in a clerk's hand and a tenth begun. It has been rained on and it has not been moved, and the mortar of the slab is fresh.
a1_cairn_a: Nine names read off station-book pages in a wind that wants them. All nine are Wardens. All nine signed in at the fourth station this winter, in the correct form, with times. None of them signed out at the fourth station or anywhere else on the road, and the tenth name is only half written.
e_a1_cairn_1: The cairn is taken apart properly to see what it was built over, which takes twenty minutes of careful work. Under the slab is a station book with four hundred pages in it, and under the book is a hand, and the hand is still holding the pen it was signing with when the slab went on.
a1_wind: The wind gap above the third station is eighty feet of dwarf cutting through which the spine funnels an entire valley's air, and has done since the founding. It arrives in cycles rather than gusts. Ossa has crossed it eleven times and starts counting the cycle out loud before anybody asks her to.
a1_wind_a: The lull is counted out by somebody who has crossed this gap eleven times, and then used. Ninety seconds, she says, and it is ninety seconds, and the whole company is through with eleven to spare. On the far side she goes back to counting under her breath and does not stop for a mile.
a1_wind_b: Eighty feet of crawling on a roped line with the wind taking the breath sideways out of everybody's mouths. It works. Nobody discusses it afterwards, and Dellach in particular does not discuss it, having spent the last twenty feet of it on his stomach with his shield over his head.
a1_wind_c: The barrow goes through first on a line and arrives on the far side upside down and one cask lighter, which is a better outcome than any of the alternatives available. The cask is somewhere below the gap. Halt watches it go and says a sentence that Nyre declines to write in her book.
e_a1_wind_1: The gap is walked upright by people who have been on a spine road for a day and a half and believe they understand it. The gust arrives at the sixtieth foot. The dwarves cut this gap to survive that gust and cut it for nothing else at all, which is a distinction the company works out too late.
e_a1_wind_2: A return trip into the gap for the barrow, in what looks like the next lull and is not. What it is is the pause the cycle makes before its worst, which Ossa knows and does not have time to say. Her count reaches four before the noise takes the rest of the sentence off the ridge.
a1_ice: The ice stair is four hundred dwarf steps up the shoulder, glazed a finger thick, with an iron handline that stops at the halfway post for reasons nobody has recorded. Outside the handline there is two thousand feet of nothing. The steps are cut deep and the glaze has filled every one of them level.
a1_ice_a: Two hours of step-cutting with a pick, one person working and four standing in the cold waiting to move up. It is the slow way. It is also the way people come back from, which Vurma says once at the bottom and does not need to say again anywhere on the stair.
a1_ice_b: The handline to the halfway post and crampons above it, which is fast and puts the whole company's weight in turn on eleven inches of dwarf ironwork that the mountain has been working at for nine hundred years. It holds. Everybody looks at the fixing bolt on the way past, and nobody says anything about it.
e_a1_ice_1: The rock beside the stair is taken instead of the stair, and it is sound rock with good holds. It also carries a nine-hundred-year glaze of black ice on every one of those holds, indistinguishable from wet stone until a gloved hand is already committed to it. The second hold is where the company finds that out.
a1_glass: The glass gallery runs the road inside the mountain for a mile, and the wall on the right is ice rather than rock: clear ice, nine inches of it, with lamp niches burning steadily on the far side. The niches are dwarf-cut and the lamps in them are lit, and there is no way in to any of them from this side.
a1_glass_a: A niche is chipped open through nine inches of clear ice, which takes twenty minutes and produces a lamp with clean oil and a trimmed wick behind it. There is no passage behind the niche and no soot on its roof. Nothing at all in the gallery explains how either the oil or the trimming got there this winter.
a1_glass_b: A mile of gallery walked with the company's own lamps hooded, past nine niches burning behind nine inches of ice. Nobody speaks after the fourth one. At the far end Ossa says that her father counted eleven niches on this stretch and that she has counted nine every time she has walked it since.
a1_glass_c: An hour at the gallery mouth waiting out the ninth hour, and the file passes inside: nine lamps, unhurried, in step, and a count that does not go up. From outside, through nine inches of ice, it is a procession of lights and a rhythm. The company watches the whole thing without one person suggesting they go in.
e_a1_glass_1: The wall ice is broken for a shortcut through a mile of gallery, which is nine inches of ice that has been holding the mountain's meltwater off this road since the founding. It stops holding it in the fourth minute. The company is halfway through the breach when the gallery starts filling behind them.
e_a1_glass_2: A lamp is taken out of a niche behind nine inches of ice, because it is a lamp and the company needs lamps. The nine niches of the gallery go dark in order behind them. The count that starts in the dark afterwards is not on the far side of the ice, and it is closer than the far wall.
a1_crevasse: The ice has pulled away from the rock across the whole shoulder, leaving a crevasse forty feet down to blue and no bottom that a lamp can find. There is a snow bridge at the narrow end and a Guild ladder frozen into the ice at the wide one, with its lashings still on it.
a1_crevasse_a: The Guild's ladder is chopped free and laid across, and it holds five people and a barrow, which it does not deserve to do. Vurma refuses to look at it while anybody is on it and refuses to explain why until the last person is over, at which point she explains at some length.
a1_crevasse_b: The snow bridge is crossed roped, one at a time, on hands and knees. The fourth person over puts a leg through it and is pulled out by the harness in eleven seconds, which is nine seconds faster than the drill and about as fast as anybody has ever done it.
e_a1_crevasse_1: Four feet is jumped at the crevasse's narrow end by somebody who has been walking uphill in crampons for six hours, which is the problem. The landing lip is snow over nothing, and it has been waiting all winter for exactly that piece of reasoning to arrive and put its full weight on it.
a1_icelamps: The ice-lamp station above the crevasse has nine brackets cut into the ice wall itself, all nine burning, and a station book on a chain under a slate roof. The book is dry. The last four weeks of it have been signed by the same hand every single day, at the same time, to the minute.
a1_icelamps_a: Four weeks of station book read in a wind that wants the pages, holding them down with both gloves. The same hand every day. The same time to the minute. And the hours for each day written in the column before the day they were kept, which means the book is a schedule rather than a record.
e_a1_icelamps_1: The station book comes off its chain and goes into a pack, because it is evidence and evidence is what wins arguments with Wardens. It is Warden property and the only record of who has come up this road. It is missed at the next station, by the person who has been signing it, within the hour.
a1_village: Highfold is the first of the counted villages on the shelf road: forty houses, a green, and nine lamps burning on that green at midday for no reason the daylight explains. The headman's wife counts the company in at the gate, out loud, and she does not stop counting when she reaches five.
a1_village_a: The question is asked plainly on a village green and answered just as plainly by a woman who has lived inside the arrangement her whole life. The lamps are the rent. Highfold has paid it since her grandmother's time, it is paid in the ninth month, and she is puzzled that anybody official has finally come to ask.
a1_village_b: Bread, cheese and a barn floor bought for coin, with no questions asked in either direction. The village goes about its afternoon around the company as though the company were weather. Two children follow Ossa's lamp-pole about all afternoon, and one of them can already recite the station hours.
e_a1_village_1: Nine lamps are ordered out on Warden authority in a village that has kept them lit for nine generations. Forty people do not argue, and do not put them out, and do not let the company leave before the ninth hour. They are apologetic about all three of those things, and entirely immovable on the last one.
a1_shrine: The village shrine is a dwarf road-marker older than the village, with a Reckoning cross fixed to its face by four modern nails. Under the cross the marker's base carries a tally cut in groups of nine, and the tally goes back further than the cross, the village, or the order that put the cross there.
a1_shrine_a: The marker's base is read with a glove off: nine hundred years of groups, in the same system the company has now seen at four doors. The last group has eight strokes cut and a ninth begun. Over the top of all of it somebody has fixed a Reckoning cross, and the nails are less than ten years old.
e_a1_shrine_1: A Reckoning cross is prised off a dwarf marker in front of a counted village, which manages to be sacrilege to two orders at once. Forty people watch it happen without moving. The company spends the ninth hour explaining itself on a village green, which is precisely where nobody in Highfold wants anybody standing at that hour.
a1_barn: The barn at the village's upper end is the one thing the headman's wife asked the company not to open. There are nine bootprints in the mud of its doorway going in. There are none at all coming out, and the mud is soft enough that a print from yesterday would still be sharp.
a1_barn_a: The barn opens on nine of them standing in the straw in Warden cloaks, drained to paper, hands folded, boots paired at the wall. The fourth from the left turns its head with the deliberate courtesy of a clerk noticing a visitor at a counter. Nobody in the company gets as far as raising a weapon.
a1_barn_b: An hour in the lane watching a barn door, and at the hour's turn the door opens from the inside. Nine of them come out and go along the shelf road in file, unhurried, in the wrong direction for a village and the right one for the road above it. The barn door closes itself afterwards.
a1_barn_c: The roof beams are counted from the lane, which gives nine, and the barn's footprint is paced out along the wall, which gives nine by nine. It is a dwarf building with a village barn's roof on it. Nobody in Highfold will say who built it, and two people say, unprompted, that it was here first.
e_a1_barn_1: The barn is fired where it stands with nine of them in the straw, and it goes up beautifully, and the straw makes it quick. Forty villagers watch from their doorways without any expression at all. Then they go back inside, and at the ninth hour the company understands what the barn was for and what it was holding.
e_a1_barn_2: A question is asked of something standing in straw, and it is answered: a station name, a date, and then the captain's own name with the correct rank and the correct company. The other eight turn their heads together to hear the rest of the exchange, and there is a great deal of the rest of it.
a1_headman: The headman of Highfold has been expecting somebody official for nine years and has a ledger ready on the table for when they came. He wants the company to carry his village's accounts down to Sarnhold and to be witnessed accepting them. He has had the witnessing clause written out for six of those nine years.
a1_headman_a: A village ledger is taken and witnessed on the green in front of forty people, which takes eleven minutes and adds four pounds to the barrow. It puts Highfold's arrangement into the Warden record for the first time since the arrangement was made. Two households ask to have their own names added while the ink is out.
a1_headman_b: The refusal is given honestly, with a promise to send a Warden clerk in the spring. The headman has heard that promise from two previous officials and writes today's date beside it in his ledger anyway, which is not sarcasm. It is a record, and he keeps records, and that is the whole problem.
e_a1_headman_1: The headman's ledger is read on his own green and the company's arrival is in it, in advance, in the hand that signs the station books. Forty people are standing between the green and the road by the time anybody has finished reading the entry. None of them is armed and all of them are apologetic.
a1_adit: The smugglers' adit is a dwarf drainage bore that runs under the first four stations: four feet high, half flooded, entirely unlit, with a Guild rope still rigged in the entrance and its far end out of sight. The Guild's own charts do not admit it exists. The scree field's wheel-track came from somewhere near here.
a1_adit_a: The Guild's rope is taken on trust, which works for six hundred feet. Then it ends in a splice somebody made in the dark, over water of unknown depth, with the tail of the original rope hanging free beside it. Whoever made that splice was standing where the company is standing now, and was not going on.
a1_adit_b: The company's own line is rigged and paid out properly, which costs three hours in a four-foot bore and means everybody comes out at the same time as everybody else. Halt complains for the first hour and stops in the second, when the line takes his weight at the first roof-fall and holds it.
a1_adit_c: Kettle goes in first and comes back in forty minutes with three roof-falls counted, two crawlable and one that needs digging, and an opinion about the water that she delivers in a single word. She also comes back with her lamp out and does not immediately explain why, and nobody presses her on it.
e_a1_adit_1: A four-foot flooded dwarf bore is taken fast, because four stations is four days and the door is nine. The third roof-fall arrives at chest-deep water in the dark with the whole company already past the second one. There is no room to turn round in a four-foot bore, which everybody has known since the entrance.
e_a1_adit_2: Somebody else's splice is trusted a second time, in the dark, over water, by people who have already got away with it once. The second splice is where the first rigger stopped, and the reason he stopped is on the far side of it and has been waiting for the rope to be trusted again.
a1_drift: The adit opens into a dwarf gallery nine feet wide, and the gallery floor has been swept. Not worn: swept, recently, along its whole visible length, in a bore that nobody has officially entered since the survey. There is no broom in sight and the sweeping runs uphill and downhill in both directions.
a1_drift_a: The swept floor is followed uphill for a quarter mile to a lamp niche with a broom leaning against the wall beside it. The bristles are dry. There is a candle stub in the niche that is still warm to the back of a hand, and the sweeping continues past the niche in the same direction.
a1_drift_b: The gallery is crossed at a run and the bore re-entered on the far side, wet to the waist again inside four steps. Nobody says anything at all about the swept floor. Ilsabet writes two lines in her book about it that evening and reads them to nobody, which is how the company knows they are bad lines.
e_a1_drift_1: The swept floor is followed downhill, which is the direction the sweeping was going. After eleven minutes it arrives at what is being swept toward, and at what has been doing the sweeping, and at how long it has been at the work. All three of those answers arrive at once and none of them can be used.
a1_cache: A smugglers' cache fills a side bay: eleven crates under tarpaulin, nine of them Guild-marked and two of them marked not at all. Above the crates a lamp bracket has been screwed into dwarf stone by somebody who did not care what dwarf stone thinks about screws, and there is a fresh lamp in it.
a1_cache_a: The two unmarked crates open on founding-gauge blanks packed in straw in one, and nine lamp reservoirs in the other, filled and sealed with wax. The wax is dated. The date is a week from today, which is not a thing anybody in the company can immediately explain and not a thing anybody wants to discuss in a side bay.
a1_cache_b: A Guild crate is opened and salt beef, candles and two coils of line come out of it. Nyre leaves a note in the lid recording exactly what was removed, by whom, and under what authority, which is the sort of thing that seems absurd in a smugglers' cache and reads extremely well at an inquiry.
e_a1_cache_1: A lamp bracket is unscrewed from dwarf stone for the sake of a pint of oil, and it comes away with nine hundred years of the wall's own arrangement behind it. The bay's roof takes that personally and immediately. There is no warning at all, which is the thing dwarf stone is famous for and everybody forgets.
a1_beast: The bore widens into a chamber the survey does not show, and something that has been eating the smugglers' cache for a season lies asleep across the only way out. It is the size of a plough horse and the wrong shape for one, and its breathing sets the water in the floor moving on a slow count.
a1_beast_a: A killing is attempted on something asleep, which goes extremely well for four seconds. After that it is eleven minutes of noise in a stone chamber with a pick and a poleaxe and no room at all to swing either properly. It ends. Two people can walk afterwards without help, and the thing does not get up.
a1_beast_b: The ledge above the exit is eleven inches wide and taken in the dark with the thing breathing underneath at a pace that does not change while five people go over the top of it. Nobody breathes on the ledge. Everybody breathes at the far end, which is when the pace underneath changes.
a1_beast_c: The last of the Guild's salt beef goes down eleven feet from the exit, and the transaction is accepted without any negotiation. The company walks past something that watches them go with its chin on its paws, and Kettle says afterwards that the whole arrangement felt professional, which is the word that stays with everybody.
e_a1_beast_1: A thing is woken deliberately in a stone chamber with one exit, by a company that wanted the fight on its own terms. In a room with one exit the terms belong to whatever lives in the room. It takes four minutes for that to become clear and rather less than that for it to stop mattering.
e_a1_beast_2: The wounded thing is finished rather than left, which is correct practice and takes four minutes longer than the company has. The noise of the first four seconds has been travelling up the bore the whole time, and something at the top of the bore has been coming down toward it since the second minute.
a1_bridge: The old span at the fifth station crosses two hundred feet of air on a dwarf deck with its parapet long gone. The deck is sound. A Guild sign at each end forbids more than two people on it at once, in three languages, and the sign at the near end has been repainted this year.
a1_bridge_a: Three crossings of two, done slowly, with the deck ringing under boots in a way that stone should not ring. Nobody looks over the edge, which takes some doing on a deck with no parapet. On the far side Hask says that the sign is not a Guild sign at all and shows them the mason's mark.
a1_bridge_b: The whole company crosses at once against a Guild sign's advice, and the deck carries them, because dwarves built it to carry a train. It costs a cask off the barrow when the deck's ring changes pitch in the middle and everybody moves at once. Nobody suggests doing that again on the way back.
e_a1_bridge_1: The ford below the old span is a spine river in a thaw. It is crossable in late summer by people who know it. In the second week of a thaw it is crossable by nobody at all, which the company establishes with four people already committed and the fifth on the bank paying out a rope that is not long enough.
a1_watchtower: The fifth station's watchtower is empty, its door barred from the outside, and its lamp lit. Inside, the signing book lies open on the table at a page dated tomorrow, with the ink dry. There is a stove that has been out for a week and a chair that has not, and the tower is warm.
a1_watchtower_a: Tomorrow's page, read today: five arrivals entered in advance in a clerk's hand, with times against each. One of the entries is the company's own number. The time against it has not happened yet, and the ink of it is as dry as the ink of every other entry on the page.
a1_watchtower_b: Four gallons of station oil and forty feet of spare rope taken from a Warden tower and signed for in the book under today's date, which is the correct procedure. Under tomorrow's date, in the same book, in the other hand, the taking has already been recorded, along with the quantities.
e_a1_watchtower_1: A night is spent in a barred watchtower waiting for whoever writes tomorrow's page. The page is written at the ninth hour, from the inside, by a hand that comes up through the floor hatch to do it and goes back down afterwards. The company is in the room for all of it, and none of them can move.
a1_pass: The pass at nine thousand feet is the last of the road above cloud, and from it the crown gate of Kar Ashen is visible for the first time as a black notch in the ridge four miles on. Weather is building behind the summit. Ossa looks at it for a while and gives it two hours, and then revises that to one.
a1_pass_a: The pass is taken at a run in the last hour before the weather lands, and it works. It is also the point at which the mountain stops being scenery for everybody in the company at once. Nobody who was on that ridge in that hour ever describes it afterwards to anybody who was not.
a1_pass_b: A hole is dug below the pass and roofed with the tarpaulin, and five people sit in it for eleven hours while the weather goes over the top of them making a sound like a mill. Nobody sleeps. Everybody comes out able to walk, which is the entire purpose of a hole in the ground.
a1_pass_c: The high traverse round the pass adds four miles and a thousand feet of climbing and keeps the company out of the wind for all of it. Ossa says her father called it the long way and used it every single time. Her father walked this road for thirty years and died in bed, which she also mentions.
e_a1_pass_1: Hask is sent over the pass alone to find the gate road, on the reasonable grounds that he has been up twice. The weather lands between him and the company in the fourth minute. There are eleven hours of nothing afterwards, and then a clear morning, and then four days of looking that turn up his pack.
e_a1_pass_2: The storm's first hour is walked into on the strength of having beaten the pass, which is exactly the sort of reasoning that gets people onto a ridge at nine thousand feet in weather. It takes the top layer off the snow and puts it into everybody's lungs, and the company is strung out over a quarter mile inside ten minutes.
a1_camp: The last camp below the crown gate is in the lee of a dwarf revetment a mile short of the arch, and from it nine lamps are visible burning on the gate in cloud. They have been burning since the company first saw the notch. Nobody in the camp suggests that anybody is trimming them.
a1_camp_a: A real night's sleep in the lee of dwarf stonework, with a brazier, two watches and the packs in the middle. It is the last sleep on the near side of the crown gate. In the morning five people stand up able to walk to a closed door and think clearly about what to do with it.
a1_storm: The weather off the summit arrives early and arrives on the shelf road, with nine hours of daylight left and no shelter marked on any chart between here and the eighth station. Visibility goes to eleven feet in about four minutes. Ossa gets her pole onto the road's outer edge and keeps it there.
a1_storm_a: Nine miles walked roped in whiteout with a lamp-lighter's pole feeling out the road edge the entire way. It is the worst day anybody has had since the Barrow Moor and nobody is lost on it, which is entirely down to a nineteen-year-old with her father's pole and her father's method.
a1_storm_b: A hole dug in the lee of the road bank and roofed with the tarpaulin, and eleven hours of five people breathing each other's air while the spine works itself out overhead. Dellach tells the whole of a story about a siege at Rell's Gate, badly, twice, and everybody is grateful for it.
e_a1_storm_1: A run is made for the eighth station on the strength of it probably being manned. The eighth station is four hundred yards off the road on a spur, which is on the chart and not on anybody's memory of the chart. The company looks for it in whiteout for two hours, which is ninety minutes longer than the weather allows.
a1_shelter: A dwarf shelter is cut into the road bank at the eighth station: benches, a flue that draws properly, a wood store still stacked, and nine lamp brackets with nine trimmed lamps in them. The wood is dry. Somebody restocked the store recently and did not sign anything, and the shelter has been swept.
a1_shelter_a: Four hours with a fire in a dwarf flue, dry socks all round and hot water for everybody's hands. The wood store's own tally is on the wall, restocked eleven days ago according to the marks, by somebody who did not put a name to it. The tally is kept in groups of nine, like everything else on this road.
a1_wolves: The ninth station's ground has spine wolves denning in its old revetments, and four of them are sitting in the road watching the company come up. They are not hunting. They are sitting in the road, in a line, in the way that animals sit when they have been fed on a schedule at a particular place.
a1_wolves_a: Four spine wolves broken through with shields, noise and a poleaxe, which works and costs Dellach a forearm laid open to the bone. Nyre gets it closed in the road with the light going. Two of the wolves run and two do not, and nobody in the company enjoys any part of the eleven minutes.
a1_wolves_b: A mile off the road round the wolves' ground in snow to the thigh, which costs two hours and everybody's legs and not one drop of blood. Hask, who has been up this road twice, says he did the same thing both times and that the wolves have been in those revetments longer than the Wardens have been on the spine.
a1_wolves_c: Salt beef goes down in the road and the company walks through at the pace of a funeral. Four wolves eat eleven feet away without hurrying. One of them does not eat at all and watches the pack on Ilsabet's back the whole way past, and turns its head to keep watching it afterwards.
e_a1_wolves_1: One wolf is shot in the road to see what the rest do, which is a question with a well-known answer to anybody who has wintered on the spine. Four become eleven inside a minute, in open country with no cover and one shield between five people. The road at that point is nine feet wide.
e_a1_wolves_2: The runners are followed off the road and finished in their own revetment, which is thorough. It also puts five people in a dwarf ruin at dusk with the den behind them, and the den is occupied by the part of the pack that did not come out to sit in the road in the first place.
a1_ridge: The last ridge below Kar Ashen carries the road along its crest with the whole spine dropping away into cloud on both sides. The crown gate is a quarter mile above, lit, with its nine lamps clear now. Anything standing at that gate can see the entire length of the crest, and the crest has no cover on it at all.
a1_ridge_a: The north traverse below the crest is snow to the thigh and out of sight of the gate, and it takes an hour to cover a quarter mile. It arrives with the company below the arch rather than in front of it, in the shadow of the gate's own revetment, which is worth every minute of the hour.
a1_ridge_b: The crest is walked in the open in full view of a lit gate a quarter mile above, which is either confidence or a formality depending on who is watching. Nothing interrupts it. The nine lamps burn steadily the whole way and nobody comes out of the arch, and that is somehow worse than an interruption.
a1_ridge_c: Cloud is waited for and then used: forty minutes of it, and the company arrives at the gate's revetment inside the weather with nobody's lamp visible from anywhere. Vurma calls it the first competent thing anybody has done since Sarnhold, which is unfair to Ossa and everybody lets it stand anyway.
e_a1_ridge_1: A quarter mile of crest at nine thousand feet, taken at a run by five people carrying packs, in the dark. A Guild survey marked the cornice on the left hand in spring, and nobody has marked it since, and the survey is in the company's own pack in Ilsabet's shorthand copy.
e_a1_ridge_2: The traverse is pushed further to get above the gate, out onto the north face proper, which is not a route and was never a route. It resembles a ledge for its first eleven feet. After that it resembles nothing at all, and there is no way back along it in the dark for people carrying packs.
a1_crowngate: The crown gate of Kar Ashen is a dwarf arch the width of the road driven into the ridge, with nine lamps burning on nine brackets in cloud and a scraped Warden shield nailed to the post. The gate itself stands open exactly a hand's width. The bar is on the inside, set down neatly, out of the way.
